prize_parts.citation: For the development of massively parallel DNA sequencing by synthesis, based on reversible-terminator nucleotide chemistry and single-molecule detection on a surface

statement.case_for: I keep sequencing by synthesis as my preferred single-topic prize. The round-1 exchange did not weaken the core of it: a reversible-terminator nucleotide, a surface, and single-molecule fluorescence read-out are an unusually simple and general chemical solution, and the consequences are already beyond dispute, with the cost of reading DNA down by many orders of magnitude and every field of biology and medicine changed. It has been independently reproduced for two decades, so maturity is not in question. The Balasubramanian-Klenerman pair is the compact Cambridge attribution, and the citation I propose is worded around the chemistry (the terminator and the surface single-molecule detection) rather than the platform, which answers the chair's request for a sharper statement of what was invented. Among the three candidates that make up the practical field, this is the one that combines a clear new capability with full maturity.
statement.case_against: The objections are real and I have not dissolved them. Chabes, Aili, Brzezinski and Linke all ask whether this is chemistry or platform engineering and medicine, and the 1980 prize (Gilbert and Sanger) adds to that. Credit is entangled: Rothberg's 454 platform, Mayer's clustering and Ju's terminator work all have claims, and a prize that names only two Cambridge scientists will be called incomplete by some. Only I put it first, so a final vote on it would need a shift from members who currently lean to B066 or B038, and I accept that this may not happen. If the committee judges that the chemical invention cannot be separated cleanly from the engineering, I would not insist and would turn to B038.

responses.point: Linke asks me directly whether my last-place ranking of B066 reflects clinical immaturity or the attribution, and asks for a sharper statement of the chemical invention in B057.
responses.response: Both, but the attribution weighs more. The mechanism of induced proximity is solid and independently confirmed, so I do not doubt the science. What I doubt is that three names can carry a citation spanning two strands, and I would have to explain to the public why Ciulli, Gray, Sakamoto and Kim are absent while no degrader is yet approved. On your request for B057, the chemical invention is the 3'-blocked, fluorescently labelled reversible-terminator nucleotide that can be cleaved to restore a natural 3'-OH, combined with surface-attached single molecules read by total-internal-reflection fluorescence. That is a molecular design and chemistry problem, not just engineering, and the citation now says so. I accept that your concern about the border with Medicine is legitimate.

responses.point: Chabes answers my opening proposal to put Ciulli in place of Handa by arguing that cereblon is a separate mechanistic discovery that explains a drug class, and says sequencing is mature and his own second choice.
responses.response: You have convinced me on this point. Ciulli's VHL ligands and structural work made degraders drug-like, which is optimisation of the concept, whereas Handa's identification of cereblon as the thalidomide target shows the principle was already in clinical use, so Crews, Deshaies and Handa is the more defensible trio and I withdraw my substitution. This moves B066 from my last place to a listed alternative, because that attribution problem is smaller than I first thought. It does not move it ahead of B057 for me, since the lack of an approved degrader and the omission of Ciulli, Gray, Sakamoto and Kim remain. I still would not add Rothberg to B057: I have seen no priority evidence for a general method that the Cambridge chemistry did not already contain.

responses.point: Somfai argues that Buchwald-Hartwig C-N coupling is a ligand-designed general method with a two-person attribution that is clean, mature and distinct from the 2010 prize.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution and the maturity, and I stand by my round-1 view that hard amido-palladium reductive elimination required its own ligand design, so the 2010 prize does not cover it. That is why B038 is now my first alternative. My remaining hesitation is the one you and Zou both note: it is a method rather than a new capability, and Kosugi's earlier tin-amide work has to be dealt with in the citation. I rate sequencing as the more fundamental change in what scientists can do, but if the committee wants a synthetic prize with the cleanest credit, I could vote for B038.

responses.point: Aili argues that targeted protein degradation is a design principle that moves pharmacology from occupancy to event-driven removal and has the strongest opening support, with Crews, Deshaies and Handa as the core.
responses.response: The occupancy to event-driven point is the strongest argument for B066 and I accept it as a real conceptual change. Where we still differ is on timing. For me a game-changer has already shown its consequences, and the clinical verdict on degraders is still pending, whereas sequencing has no such open question. I also note that you have not answered the Ciulli, Gray, Sakamoto and Kim omission beyond conceding it. I will not argue that three supporters is not meaningful, but a count of supporters does not replace the judgment on maturity.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks Gray and Winkler's long-range electron transfer first, but notes that no one else ranked it and that Marcus theory and Dutton-Moser priority are open.
responses.response: I respect the clarity of the physical mechanism and the compact pair, and as a theorist I know how the Marcus theory sits behind it. For a prize the question is whether the experiments are a discovery distinct from that theory, and I think the answer needs the expert report. With a single supporter it cannot reach five votes. I would ask whether you could support B057 or B038 as a second choice, since you listed B057 as your own first alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts reversible-terminator sequencing as a chemical achievement rather than technology or medicine, given the 1980 prize.
Whether Rothberg, Mayer or Ju need to be named for the credit to hold, and what priority evidence would show it.
Whether B066 will be recognised before the first approved degrader, and whether a three-name trio of Crews, Deshaies and Handa is accepted as covering both PROTACs and molecular glues.
Whether the 2010 cross-coupling prize is judged to cover C-N coupling.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I am a computational biochemist with no tie to any shortlisted person, including the sequencing candidates; my Warshel-school and Uppsala ribosome connections are not close to anyone on the shortlist. Since I no longer list Car-Parrinello among my alternatives, my possible bias toward computational work is not in play. No recusal is required.
